scope: Sections 3 and 5 use modular exponentiation. The executable binary run agrees with natural powering modulo N and performs at most two modular multiplications per exponent bit.
For the Section 5 classical reduction, every reported divisor is proper, even when the order candidate is incorrect. A positive nonunit below N yields its gcd with N before order finding.

Section 5 compares the 2-adic valuations of component orders. An unsuccessful unit projects to an element with the full global order valuation under any residue-ring homomorphism to a modulus larger than two.
In a finite cyclic group of even size, multiplication by a generator changes the 2-adic valuation of the order. This supplies the local half bound for the Section 5 CRT argument.

Counting injection for the Section 5 CRT proof. Once one coordinate of a k-fold product is fixed, a generator shift that changes labels independently in every other coordinate bounds agreement by a fraction 2^(1−k).

Section 5, before Eq. (5.1). Among uniformly random units modulo every odd N > 1 with k distinct prime factors, an even order whose half-power differs from −1 occurs with probability at least 1−2^(1−k). Lean constructs the prime-power CRT decomposition from N.
Section 5, classical reduction. A good unit and its true order yield a proper divisor using the single minus-sign gcd of the modular half-power.
With t independent uniformly random units and exact orders, at most a fraction 2^(−(k−1)t) of the sample tuples produce no factor. This augments the single-trial bound before Eq. (5.1).
Section 5, random-base reduction. Uniform sampling from all 1,…,N−1 has failure fraction at most 2^(1−k), since every nonunit gives a factor immediately and the candidate is the exact order on units.
For the optional classical perfect-power step in Section 5, binary search makes exactly one power comparison per root bit and recovers any exact integer root in its initial interval.

The implementation checks candidate exponents in descending order. Its power scan returns only proper divisors, finds every exact power with exponent in its search range, and counts the worst-case number of comparisons.
Implements the Section 5 classical treatment of easy inputs. The routine returns a proper factor of every even N > 2 and every perfect power a^e with a,e ≥ 2.
The Section 5 preprocessing implementation uses at most (L−2)(L+1) power comparisons at positive input width L, with natural subtraction. This is an arithmetic operation count.
If a composite number above one survives classical preprocessing, it is odd and has at least two distinct prime factors. These are the hypotheses of Shor’s order-to-factoring reduction.
For each exponent e ≤ floor(log₂ N), all candidate powers along the binary root search fit in L·e ≤ L² bits. This certifies polynomial operand widths for the classical preprocessing comparisons.
An explicit fair-bit implementation of the random positive base draw in Section 5. Every target base has a unique accepted word of length 1+floor(log₂(N−1)) and at least half the words are accepted.
